nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: 4/4/1994.  Steve Traxler| Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Pigfish
Scientific Name: Orthopristes chrysoptera

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Haemulidae

Other Common Names:  Grunt (664), sailor's choice (327 834 867), hogfish (312), piggy perch (255), big perch (320).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Taken by seines, traps, trawls and handlines, most are marketed as live bait (791 859).  In the Gulf of Mexico, pigfish have little economic value (859).  However, in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) pigfish are the primary bait of the inshore spotted seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus, 'splatter pole' fishery.  The pigfish are collected in wire-mesh fish traps, but there are no records for this live bait fishery (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication).  Caught as a bycatch by shrimp trawlers (1028).
Recreational:  Caught on hook and line by recreational fishermen; often used as live bait (1028).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  New York (788), Massachusetts (327) and Bermuda to Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to the Yucatan peninsula (788 791 891).  Uncommon north of Virginia (945).
Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (327).  Snelson (997) reports pigfish as uncommon in the northern Indian River Lagoon (IRL) and he collected no pigfish in the Banana River.  However, The Florida Marine Research Institute commonly collects both juveniles and adults in the Banana River (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication). Additionally, Gilmore (993) commonly found pigfish in the central part of the IRL.
Life Mode:  Common in inshore waters and bays.  Many school near reefs and jetties (1028).  Reported to school with pinfish in Charlotte Harbor (789).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: Nearshore waters throughout their range and also in estuaries and other brackish areas (834 1028).  Common on intertidal flats (1028), and in shallow waters of Florida Bay (702).  Also occur offshore (303), on offshore reefs and platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, and openshelf habitats along the southeastern coast (1028).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Juvenile: Young are found in grassbeds (327).  Juveniles reported over shallow grass flats at Crystal River (581) and in the IRL (993 997).  In Charlotte Harbor, young pigfish were also common in deep water sponge or drift algae habitats (Mitchell and Adams 1993).  Young move into deeper flats and the edges of channels.
Adult: adults occur over mud and sand bottoms, in vegetated areas (315 702), and over hard substrates such as reefs and jetties (859).  Also, adults are found in deeper channel habitats of the IRL, Tampa Bay, and Charlotte Harbor (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication).

nodes.title: Egg
nodes.body:
Larvae: same as Adults.
Adult: Apparently avoid low water temperatures (255 313 581 789 859 1028).  Killed in Texas when temperatures fell to 4.5 C (489).  Moe and Martin (798) did not collect them off Pinellas County, Florida when temperatures were below 12.5 C. Totally absent at temperatures of 12 - 14 C in St. Andrews Bay, but abundant at temperatures of 16.5 to 31 C (1028).  Most abundant at Cedar Key at 25.2 C (581).  Maximum inshore abundance coincides with highest water temperatures (1028).  Collected in southwest Florida at temperatures from 19.5 to 30.6 C (603).  Reported from temperatures of 17.5 to 32.5 C in Tampa Bay (664).  Pigfish were not killed in the hypothermal mortality within the IRL during January and February, 1977 (236).

nodes.title: Juvenile
nodes.body: Adult:  Most abundant at Cedar Key when salinities averaged 25.1 % (581).  In Tampa Bay, collected at salinities of 19.1 to 35 % (664).  Not collected in Charlotte Harbor at salinities less than 15 % (789) and primarily collected at salinities above 19 %.  Additionally, Pigfish were not observed in the Peace or Myakka rivers or at the riverine/estuarine interface (Mitchell and Adams 1993).  Collected in south Florida at salinities from 17.2 to 44.4 % (603).  Taken in Louisiana at salinities as low as 6.2 % (163).  Christensen (887) collected pigfish from 4.5 % to 37.6 % in the southern part of the IRL.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Mobility and Migration Leave the shallow Gulf of Mexico waters in winter, apparently moving offshore (798 1028).  Reported to move offshore in the fall at Beaufort, NC and return in the spring (313).  Migrations appear to be related to seasonal changes in water temperature, but diurnal feeding migrations also occur (1028).  Nocturnal foraging migrations have also been reported (1028).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual with external fertilization (1028).
Mating/Spawning: Become mature in their second year (313 1033).  Spawning occurs in the spring at Cedar Key and Crystal River, Florida (581 1029).  Spawning also occurs in the spring in Texas (255).  In Tampa Bay, Springer and Woodburn (664) reported a late winter or spring spawning period.  Other spawning periods reported are: March in Alligator Harbor, Florida (1030), January through May in the eastern Gulf of Mexico (1028), March and April in Mississippi waters (224), and February through June in Texas (322).  Spawning apparently takes place in the early evening just offshore or in harbors, estuaries, and inshore banks (313 859 1028).
Fecundity: No information found.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs (0.7-0.8 mm in diameter) are buoyant, unattached and probably planktonic (313).
Juvenile: In the IRL, Snelsen (997) found juvenile pigfish starting in June and Adams (personnel communication) found juvenile pigfish recruits in March and April.
Adult:  At Crystal River, growth rates during the spring and summer have been reported as 7 to 10 mm/month for age 0 fish (581).  A spring and summer growth rate of 19.9 mm/month occurs in North Carolina (313).  Growth from October to April slows to about 3.1 mm/month at Crystal River (1029), and was reported as 5.5 mm/month at Cedar Key (581).  At Beaufort, NC, Taylor (1033) gave the following growth increments: 47 mm between age I and II, 35 mm between age II and III, and 4.2 mm between age III and IV.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae: young are planktivorous, feeding mostly on copepods (98 313 1028), but also on ostracods and small pelycepods (664).
Juvenile: juveniles feed extensively on polychaetes (98 1028).
Adult: adults are carnivorous and feed primarily on benthic invertebrates (98 859 1028), including larger crustaceans, mollusks, polychaetes, and small fish (664 1028).

Commercial:  Taken by seines, traps, trawls and handlines, most are marketed as live bait (791 859).  In the Gulf of Mexico, pigfish have little economic value (859).  However, in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) pigfish are the primary bait of the inshore spotted seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus, 'splatter pole' fishery.  The pigfish are collected in wire-mesh fish traps, but there are no records for this live bait fishery (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication).  Caught as a bycatch by shrimp trawlers (1028).
Recreational:  Caught on hook and line by recreational fishermen; often used as live bait (1028).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  New York (788), Massachusetts (327) and Bermuda to Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to the Yucatan peninsula (788 791 891).  Uncommon north of Virginia (945).
Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (327).  Snelson (997) reports pigfish as uncommon in the northern Indian River Lagoon (IRL) and he collected no pigfish in the Banana River.  However, The Florida Marine Research Institute commonly collects both juveniles and adults in the Banana River (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication). Additionally, Gilmore (993) commonly found pigfish in the central part of the IRL.
Life Mode:  Common in inshore waters and bays.  Many school near reefs and jetties (1028).  Reported to school with pinfish in Charlotte Harbor (789).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content: Nearshore waters throughout their range and also in estuaries and other brackish areas (834 1028).  Common on intertidal flats (1028), and in shallow waters of Florida Bay (702).  Also occur offshore (303), on offshore reefs and platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, and openshelf habitats along the southeastern coast (1028).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Juvenile: Young are found in grassbeds (327).  Juveniles reported over shallow grass flats at Crystal River (581) and in the IRL (993 997).  In Charlotte Harbor, young pigfish were also common in deep water sponge or drift algae habitats (Mitchell and Adams 1993).  Young move into deeper flats and the edges of channels.
Adult: adults occur over mud and sand bottoms, in vegetated areas (315 702), and over hard substrates such as reefs and jetties (859).  Also, adults are found in deeper channel habitats of the IRL, Tampa Bay, and Charlotte Harbor (Doug Adams, FMRI, personnel communication).

sections.heading: Egg
sections.content:
Larvae: same as Adults.
Adult: Apparently avoid low water temperatures (255 313 581 789 859 1028).  Killed in Texas when temperatures fell to 4.5 C (489).  Moe and Martin (798) did not collect them off Pinellas County, Florida when temperatures were below 12.5 C. Totally absent at temperatures of 12 - 14 C in St. Andrews Bay, but abundant at temperatures of 16.5 to 31 C (1028).  Most abundant at Cedar Key at 25.2 C (581).  Maximum inshore abundance coincides with highest water temperatures (1028).  Collected in southwest Florida at temperatures from 19.5 to 30.6 C (603).  Reported from temperatures of 17.5 to 32.5 C in Tampa Bay (664).  Pigfish were not killed in the hypothermal mortality within the IRL during January and February, 1977 (236).

sections.heading: Juvenile
sections.content: Adult:  Most abundant at Cedar Key when salinities averaged 25.1 % (581).  In Tampa Bay, collected at salinities of 19.1 to 35 % (664).  Not collected in Charlotte Harbor at salinities less than 15 % (789) and primarily collected at salinities above 19 %.  Additionally, Pigfish were not observed in the Peace or Myakka rivers or at the riverine/estuarine interface (Mitchell and Adams 1993).  Collected in south Florida at salinities from 17.2 to 44.4 % (603).  Taken in Louisiana at salinities as low as 6.2 % (163).  Christensen (887) collected pigfish from 4.5 % to 37.6 % in the southern part of the IRL.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content: Mobility and Migration Leave the shallow Gulf of Mexico waters in winter, apparently moving offshore (798 1028).  Reported to move offshore in the fall at Beaufort, NC and return in the spring (313).  Migrations appear to be related to seasonal changes in water temperature, but diurnal feeding migrations also occur (1028).  Nocturnal foraging migrations have also been reported (1028).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual with external fertilization (1028).
Mating/Spawning: Become mature in their second year (313 1033).  Spawning occurs in the spring at Cedar Key and Crystal River, Florida (581 1029).  Spawning also occurs in the spring in Texas (255).  In Tampa Bay, Springer and Woodburn (664) reported a late winter or spring spawning period.  Other spawning periods reported are: March in Alligator Harbor, Florida (1030), January through May in the eastern Gulf of Mexico (1028), March and April in Mississippi waters (224), and February through June in Texas (322).  Spawning apparently takes place in the early evening just offshore or in harbors, estuaries, and inshore banks (313 859 1028).
Fecundity: No information found.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Eggs (0.7-0.8 mm in diameter) are buoyant, unattached and probably planktonic (313).
Juvenile: In the IRL, Snelsen (997) found juvenile pigfish starting in June and Adams (personnel communication) found juvenile pigfish recruits in March and April.
Adult:  At Crystal River, growth rates during the spring and summer have been reported as 7 to 10 mm/month for age 0 fish (581).  A spring and summer growth rate of 19.9 mm/month occurs in North Carolina (313).  Growth from October to April slows to about 3.1 mm/month at Crystal River (1029), and was reported as 5.5 mm/month at Cedar Key (581).  At Beaufort, NC, Taylor (1033) gave the following growth increments: 47 mm between age I and II, 35 mm between age II and III, and 4.2 mm between age III and IV.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae: young are planktivorous, feeding mostly on copepods (98 313 1028), but also on ostracods and small pelycepods (664).
Juvenile: juveniles feed extensively on polychaetes (98 1028).
Adult: adults are carnivorous and feed primarily on benthic invertebrates (98 859 1028), including larger crustaceans, mollusks, polychaetes, and small fish (664 1028).
